title: Circular lists: where the loop stops
summary: The last node points back at the first. Loops stop when they get back to head, not at NULL.

checkpoints.text: A circle of one: the only node points at itself. There is no NULL anywhere in a circular list.
Adding 3. The walk to the last node cannot stop at NULL, so it stops when the next node would be `head` again.
The new last node points back at `head`, closing the loop: 1 → 2 → 3 → 1.

`cur` is back at `head` after visiting every node once, so the loop ends. A `while` loop that tested `cur != head` first would stop before printing anything; `do ... while` prints first and tests after.
1 2 3 (back to 1). Circular lists suit things that repeat, like taking turns in round-robin scheduling or a playlist on repeat.
